units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS
I have still the mask.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: It makes your eyes lovelier.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Thank you. Come.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Sees MRS. ARBUTHNOT’S letter on table , and takes it up and looks at envelope .
What a curious handwriting! It reminds me of the handwriting of a woman I used to know years ago.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Who?
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Oh! no one. No one in particular. A woman of no importance.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Throws letter down , and passes up the steps of the terrace with MRS. ALLONBY.
They smile at each other .
Drawing-room at Hunstanton , after dinner , lamps lit .
Door L.C. Door R.C.
Ladies seated on sofas .
What a comfort it is to have got rid of the men for a little!
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Yes; men persecute us dreadfully, don’t they?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Persecute us? I wish they did.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: My dear!
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: The annoying thing is that the wretches can be perfectly happy without us. That is why I think it is every woman’s duty never to leave them alone for a single moment, except during this short breathing space after dinner; without which I believe we poor women would be absolutely worn to shadows.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Enter Servants with coffee .
Worn to shadows, dear?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Yes, Lady Hunstanton. It is such a strain keeping men up to the mark. They are always trying to escape from us.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: It seems to me that it is we who are always trying to escape from them. Men are so very, very heartless. They know their power and use it.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Takes coffee from Servant .
What stuff and nonsense all this about men is! The thing to do is to keep men in their proper place.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: But what is their proper place, Lady Caroline?
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Looking after their wives, Mrs. Allonby.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Takes coffee from Servant .
Really? And if they’re not married?
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: If they are not married, they should be looking after a wife. It’s perfectly scandalous the amount of bachelors who are going about society. There should be a law passed to compel them all to marry within twelve months.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Refuses coffee .
But if they’re in love with some one who, perhaps, is tied to another?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: In that case, Lady Stutfield, they should be married off in a week to some plain respectable girl, in order to teach them not to meddle with other people’s property.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: I don’t think that we should ever be spoken of as other people’s property. All men are married women’s property. That is the only true definition of what married women’s property really is. But we don’t belong to any one.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Oh, I am so very, very glad to hear you say so.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: But do you really think, dear Caroline, that legislation would improve matters in any way? I am told that, nowadays, all the married men live like bachelors, and all the bachelors like married men.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I certainly never know one from the other.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Oh, I think one can always know at once whether a man has home claims upon his life or not. I have noticed a very, very sad expression in the eyes of so many married men.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Ah, all that I have noticed is that they are horribly tedious when they are good husbands, and abominably conceited when they are not.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Well, I suppose the type of husband has completely changed since my young days, but I’m bound to state that poor dear Hunstanton was the most delightful of creatures, and as good as gold.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Ah, my husband is a sort of promissory note; I’m tired of meeting him.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: But you renew him from time to time, don’t you?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Oh no, Lady Caroline. I have only had one husband as yet. I suppose you look upon me as quite an amateur.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: With your views on life I wonder you married at all.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: So do I.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: My dear child, I believe you are really very happy in your married life, but that you like to hide your happiness from others.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I assure you I was horribly deceived in Ernest.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Oh, I hope not, dear. I knew his mother quite well. She was a Stratton, Caroline, one of Lord Crowland’s daughters.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Victoria Stratton? I remember her perfectly. A silly fair-haired woman with no chin.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE
